abstract: I consider a risk-sharing game with limited commitment, and study how the discount factor above which perfect risk sharing is self-enforcing in the long run depends on agents' risk aversion and the riskiness of their endowment. When agents face no aggregate risk, a mean-preserving spread may destroy the sustainability of perfect risk sharing if each agent's endowment may take more than three values. With aggregate risk the same can happen with only two possible endowment realizations. With respect to risk aversion the intuitive comparative statics result holds without aggregate risk, but it holds only under strong assumptions in the presence of aggregate risk.
summary_en: How does the sustainability of risk-sharing in informal communities depend on members' risk aversion and the riskiness of their incomes? Laczó analyses a risk-sharing game with limited commitment and shows that even mean-preserving spreads in the income distribution can destroy perfect risk-sharing — particularly when there are more than three possible income realisations. With aggregate risk, this can happen with just two realisations. The intuitive comparative-statics result for risk aversion (more risk-averse agents share more) holds in the absence of aggregate risk, but breaks down with aggregate risk. The paper identifies tight conditions under which standard risk-sharing intuitions fail.
data_used: Theoretical model — limited-commitment risk-sharing game with two agents and varying income distributions. No primary dataset.
policy_relevance: Foundational result for understanding informal risk-sharing in Hungarian rural communities and Roma settlements where formal insurance is limited. The paper warns that standard intuitions about risk-aversion-driven mutual insurance may not apply in practice when income shocks are correlated. Useful framework for academic and policy analysis at KRTK and the Hungarian Charitable Service.
title: Does risk sharing increase with risk aversion and risk when commitment is limited?
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
